explanations.answer: It gloats and expects to gain
explanations.explanation: Tyre looks at Jerusalem in ruins and says, “Aha!” That is not a sympathy card, baker. The city says, “…now that she lies in ruins I will be filled…” (Ezekiel 26:2). I think Tyre sees a door swinging open for itself.

Nobody in this verse is packing a care package. Tyre doesn't mourn at all. It says, “Aha! The gate to the nations is broken…” (Ezekiel 26:2). That sounds like a city counting what it might gain, and I think that's the problem.

explanations.answer: It panics and shuts its gates
explanations.explanation: No gates are slamming in this verse. Tyre says the gate to the nations “has swung open to me” (Ezekiel 26:2). Tyre isn't scared of Jerusalem's fall. It says “I will be filled,” so it's expecting to gain.

I get why someone would hope so, but listen to how God answers. He says, “Behold, O Tyre, I am against you…” (Ezekiel 26:3). That is the opposite of being on her side. After the “Aha!” comes the “against you.”
God doesn't take Tyre's side. He says, “Behold, O Tyre, I am against you…” (Ezekiel 26:3). Then He says He will raise up many nations against her. Tyre said “Aha!” and God answered right away.

God says, “They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers.” (Ezekiel 26:4). Those walls were Tyre's big defense, and they're the first thing to go. Waves don't ask permission, and neither do these nations.

These nations aren't showing up with toolbelts and a cheerful attitude. God says, “They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers.” (Ezekiel 26:4). Demolish is the opposite of repair, and the text says it right there.

Nobody is posting a security detail at Tyre's walls. God says the nations “will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers.” (Ezekiel 26:4). They're coming against the city, so they aren't coming to protect it.

God says, “She will become a place to spread nets in the sea…” (Ezekiel 26:5). Once the soil is scraped off and only bare rock is left, there's room for something humble. A city with proud towers ends up as a spot to spread nets.
Nobody is pitching a campsite here. God says Tyre will become “a place to spread nets in the sea” (Ezekiel 26:5). A bare rock in the water is not the place you'd pick for a weekend of camping.
Grain needs soil, and God just said He will “scrape the soil from her” (Ezekiel 26:4). A bare rock is not a farm. What God says gets spread there is nets (Ezekiel 26:5).
God says, “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” (Ezekiel 26:6). After all of this, the point is who God is. It isn't a lesson about Tyre's résumé. It's about Him.
It's a decent guess, but that isn't what verse 6 says. God says, “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” The thing they come to know is about Him. I'd keep my eyes on that line.
Verse 6 doesn't mention Tyre's wisdom at all. God says, “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” (Ezekiel 26:6). What they will know is who He is.
God says, “Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings…” (Ezekiel 26:7). The name is right there in the verse. God says He is the One bringing him.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, is a different royal from the one in this verse. God names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Ezekiel 26:7). It's a good guess to mix up two big-name kings. Still, the text has its own name, and I'd stick with it.

Cyrus, king of Persia, isn't the name in this verse. God says, “Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezekiel 26:7). Same kind of title, different king. Check the name and you're set.

God says, “He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls…” (Ezekiel 26:9). Rams, plural, so he isn't knocking politely. The ramp and the shields are how he gets close, and the rams do the pounding.

Flaming arrows aren't in this verse. God says Nebuchadnezzar will direct “the blows of his battering rams against your walls” (Ezekiel 26:9). He also says he'll tear down her towers with his axes. The text sticks to rams and axes.
No ladders get mentioned here. God says, “He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls…” (Ezekiel 26:9). The text has him pounding the walls. Nobody is climbing over them.
God says, “…your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots.” (Ezekiel 26:10). The walls shake from the noise alone. That's a LOUD army, friend.

It is true, so this one slips by. God says that when Nebuchadnezzar enters Tyre's gates, “your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots.” (Ezekiel 26:10). The text says the walls shake from the noise alone.

That's the opposite of what God says. He says the army “will slaughter your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.” (Ezekiel 26:11). Those pillars look mighty, and they still come down.
The pillars don't stay up. God says, “…your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.” (Ezekiel 26:11). Mighty or not, they go down.

God says they will “throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.” (Ezekiel 26:12). Tyre sits in the sea, so I think the water is right there waiting. The walls and the beautiful homes end up in it.
Tyre's stones aren't headed for a valley. God says they will “throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.” (Ezekiel 26:12). Think sea, not hills.
A plain isn't mentioned. God says the stones, timber and soil get thrown “into the water.” (Ezekiel 26:12). Everything that made up Tyre goes into the sea.

God says, “So I will silence the sound of your songs, and the music of your lyres will no longer be heard.” (Ezekiel 26:13). A lyre is a stringed instrument, and its music stops. A city that was full of music goes quiet.
Nobody is turning up the volume on Tyre. God says, “I will silence the sound of your songs…” (Ezekiel 26:13). The music goes the other way. It's gone.
The songs don't make it through. God says, “…the music of your lyres will no longer be heard.” (Ezekiel 26:13). Silenced, not spared.
I know it's tempting to hope for a comeback. But God says, “You will never be rebuilt…” (Ezekiel 26:14). He says that right after calling her a bare rock for fishing nets.
God says it plainly: “You will never be rebuilt…” (Ezekiel 26:14). He repeats that she will be a bare rock and a place to spread the fishing nets. No rebuilding is promised.

God says, “All the princes of the sea will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments.” (Ezekiel 26:16). Those are people used to sitting high, and now they come down. I think a news like this would shake anybody's sense of being in charge.

No rescue fleet shows up in this verse. God says the princes of the sea “will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments.” (Ezekiel 26:16). They sit on the ground, trembling. They aren't sailing anywhere.
Nobody is throwing a party. God says the princes will sit on the ground, “trembling every moment, appalled over you.” (Ezekiel 26:16). Then they lament for her. This is a very quiet room.
God says they will sit on the ground, “trembling every moment, appalled over you.” (Ezekiel 26:16). They are clothed with terror. Even with robes off, they are shaking.
Nobody laughs in this verse. God says the princes will sit on the ground, “trembling every moment, appalled over you.” (Ezekiel 26:16). It's a heavy scene, and I think this is one to take seriously.
No bragging here. The princes sit on the ground “trembling every moment, appalled over you.” (Ezekiel 26:16). A boast would take a bit more calm than they have.
In their lament they call her “she who was powerful on the sea…” (Ezekiel 26:17). They also call her a “city of renown inhabited by seafaring men.” Tyre's strength was out on the water.
Farmland doesn't make their lament. They cry about “a city of renown inhabited by seafaring men—she who was powerful on the sea…” (Ezekiel 26:17). The princes remember her on the water.
Temples aren't mentioned in the lament. The princes say, “…she who was powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples!” (Ezekiel 26:17). They remember her sea power.
That isn't how the lament remembers her. The princes say Tyre's people “imposed terror on all peoples!” (Ezekiel 26:17). That's about terror, not peace.
The lament doesn't say peace. It says Tyre was “powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples!” (Ezekiel 26:17). Terror is the word they use.

God says, “…when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you…” (Ezekiel 26:19). Tyre sits in the sea, so the waters come right to her door. The city that ruled the water ends up under it.
No sand dunes in this verse. God says, “…when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you…” (Ezekiel 26:19). It's the deep and the mighty waters, so it's wet, not dry.
Mountains don't rise up here. God says, “…I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you…” (Ezekiel 26:19). The sea does the covering.
The text goes the other way. God says Tyre will be brought down “so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living.” (Ezekiel 26:20). That's no splendor.
God says she will be brought down “so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living.” (Ezekiel 26:20). No people living there, and no splendor.

God says, “You will be sought, but will never be found…” (Ezekiel 26:21). Folks can look all they want. It's like a cookie box left out at a party, and I'm not even exaggerating, friend. Tyre will be no more.

explanations.answer: She will be found in ruins
explanations.explanation: Even ruins don't turn up in this verse. God says, “You will be sought, but will never be found…” (Ezekiel 26:21). The search goes on and finds nothing. That is what the Lord GOD declares.

No comeback tour is promised. God says, “You will be sought, but will never be found…” (Ezekiel 26:21). In verse 20 He also says she will no longer be “set in splendor in the land of the living.” Splendor is off the table.
